title: New York Attorney General
area: Statewide — all of New York State

context.text: Both parties' primaries for this race, scheduled for June 23, 2026, were canceled because each candidate was unopposed: incumbent Letitia James advanced from the Democratic and Working Families Party primaries, and Saritha Komatireddy advanced from the Republican and Conservative Party primaries.
A September 2026 Siena University poll of likely voters found James leading Komatireddy 52% to 39%, with 10% undecided (margin of error ±3.9%).

candidates.name: Letitia James
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the Democratic and Working Families Party primaries unopposed; both primaries were canceled.
candidates.currentRole: Attorney General of New York (since January 1, 2019)

summary.text: Letitia James is the incumbent Democratic Attorney General of New York, seeking a third full term. Since taking office in 2019 she has pursued civil fraud litigation against Donald Trump and the Trump Organization, dozens of lawsuits against Trump administration policies on immigration, health care and federal funding, and consumer-protection settlements against corporations including Meta and Capital One. In 2025 she was federally indicted on mortgage-fraud charges brought by the Trump-era Justice Department; the case was dismissed and two subsequent grand juries declined to re-indict her.

background.text: Earned a bachelor's degree from the City University of New York and a law degree from Howard University.
Served on the New York City Council representing Brooklyn's 35th District from 2004 to 2013.
Served as New York City Public Advocate from 2014 to 2018, the first African American woman to be elected to and hold citywide office in New York City.
Elected Attorney General of New York in 2018 and re-elected in 2022, defeating Michael Henry 54.6% to 45.3%.

priorities.text: Protecting the 2026 elections from what her campaign describes as federal efforts to federalize voting, including opposing the SAVE Act and challenging a presidential executive order on election administration.
Public safety, including efforts against gun violence, illegal firearms and "ghost guns"; her campaign says gun buyback and enforcement efforts have taken more than 9,600 guns off New York streets.
Holding the Trump administration accountable, citing lawsuits and other legal action to protect New Yorkers' rights and funding for health care, public education and jobs.
Consumer protection, including legislative advocacy in Albany for the FAIR Business Practices Act and enforcement actions against corporations.
Housing, described on her campaign site as "a decades-long track record of protecting housing rights for vulnerable New Yorkers."

positions.summary: Has led multistate coalitions defending access to the abortion medication mifepristone, including an amicus brief asking the U.S. Supreme Court to stay a Fifth Circuit ruling that would have reinstated in-person dispensing requirements.
positions.quote: Forcing patients to obtain mifepristone in person will not make anyone safer.

positions.summary: Campaign describes ongoing work against gun violence and illegal firearms, citing more than 9,600 guns taken off New York streets through buyback and enforcement efforts.

Defended New York's Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, which bars local law enforcement from entering 287(g) cooperation agreements with ICE, saying it keeps public-safety resources focused on crime rather than immigration enforcement.

Sued the Trump administration's HHS and CMS over a rule imposing new Medicaid work requirements, arguing it would strip coverage from roughly 475,000 New Yorkers and put $17.5 billion in federal Medicaid funding at risk.
positions.quote: This rule would create needless barriers for some of our most vulnerable neighbors.

positions.summary: Launched a "de facto" rent-stabilization compliance program and filed the program's first lawsuits against two Brooklyn landlords in June 2026, seeking rent-stabilized leases, overcharge restitution with 9% interest, and civil penalties.

record.text: Won affirmation from the Appellate Division, First Department, on August 21, 2025, of the finding that Donald Trump, the Trump Organization, and two of his children are liable for fraud in the state's civil fraud case; the court also upheld injunctive relief restricting their business operations in New York. James stated she would seek appeal to the Court of Appeals over the earlier reduction of the financial penalty.

Was indicted in October 2025 on federal bank-fraud and false-statement charges related to a 2020 home purchase; the case was dismissed in November 2025 after a judge ruled the prosecuting U.S. attorney was illegally appointed, and a federal grand jury in Virginia twice declined, in December 2025, to return a new indictment against her.

Joined a coalition of 51 attorneys general in a settlement with Meta of up to $17.1 billion (New York's share $819 million to $1.15 billion), announced August 26, 2026, requiring new time limits, notification restrictions and content protections for users under 18 on Facebook and Instagram.

Joined a coalition of 40 states and the District of Columbia in a $700 million settlement with subprime auto lender Credit Acceptance Corporation, announced September 17, 2026, including more than $630 million in consumer debt relief and about $34 million for roughly 2,500 New York consumers.

Commended a $425 million class-action settlement with Capital One, announced January 12, 2026, after having led a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general opposing an earlier, less favorable proposed settlement over allegations the bank misled 360 Savings account customers out of higher interest payments; about $34 million goes to New York consumers.

Joined a coalition of 25 states and the District of Columbia suing the Trump administration's HHS and CMS on June 29, 2026, to block a rule imposing new Medicaid work and eligibility-verification requirements, arguing it would strip coverage from about 475,000 New Yorkers.

Led a 22-state coalition amicus brief on May 4, 2026, asking the U.S. Supreme Court to stay a Fifth Circuit ruling that would have reinstated in-person dispensing requirements for the abortion medication mifepristone.

Filed the first lawsuits under her office's de facto rent-stabilization compliance program on June 16, 2026, against two Brooklyn landlords accused of failing to register rent-stabilized buildings with New York State Homes and Community Renewal and of attempting to illegally evict tenants and violating tenant-harassment laws.

Intervened in her official capacity as a defendant in Trucking Association of New York v. Metropolitan Transportation Authority, a suit challenging Manhattan's congestion pricing program, filing a motion to dismiss the amended complaint on July 11, 2025.

candidates.name: Saritha Komatireddy
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the Republican and Conservative Party primaries unopposed; both primaries were canceled.

summary.text: Saritha Komatireddy is the Republican and Conservative Party nominee for Attorney General, running a law-and-order campaign against incumbent Letitia James. A former federal prosecutor in the Eastern District of New York for more than a decade and later chief of staff of the Drug Enforcement Administration, she has not previously held elected office. She has not been elected to office before; if elected she would be the first Republican New York Attorney General since Dennis Vacco left office in 1999.

background.text: Graduated cum laude from Harvard University and magna cum laude from Harvard Law School, where she served on the Harvard Law Review.
Clerked for then-Judge Brett Kavanaugh on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, 2009–2010.

Served as an Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Eastern District of New York from 2013 to 2019, prosecuting terrorism, cybercrime, narcotics, money-laundering and foreign-corruption cases, including cases against alleged al-Qaida, ISIS and Mexican drug-cartel figures.

Nominated by President Trump in 2020 to a judgeship on the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York; the nomination was returned to the president, unconfirmed, at the end of the Senate session in January 2021.
Served as Chief of Staff of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, and later became a partner at the law firm Holtzman Vogel and a lecturer at Columbia Law School.

priorities.text: Prosecuting crime and supporting law enforcement, including redirecting the Attorney General's office to devote more of its roughly 700 attorneys to criminal prosecution rather than police-misconduct investigations.
priorities.quote: The attorney general has more people assigned to investigate cops than investigate criminals, and that's a problem.

priorities.text: Reducing homelessness and untreated severe mental illness, including a plan to build residential treatment centers statewide and launch an Office of Civil Commitment to lead a stronger response to severe mental illness.

Fraud prevention, citing a report that ranked New York's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit among the worst in the nation under James and pledging to add prosecutors, pursue fraud and recover taxpayer dollars for patients and seniors.
Redirecting an estimated $3 billion in opioid-settlement funds from harm-reduction programs toward residential drug-treatment facilities.
priorities.quote: We shouldn't be using money designed to combat the opioid crisis to fund drug use.

positions.summary: Says the Attorney General's office should prioritize supporting district attorneys, sheriffs and police over investigating law enforcement, and would shift office resources toward criminal prosecution.
positions.quote: The attorney general has more people assigned to investigate cops than investigate criminals, and that's a problem.

candidates.researchNotes: Komatireddy has not previously held elected office, so there is no record of votes, sponsored bills or official actions to list. Her positions on several issue areas in this guide (abortion, immigration policy beyond the 287(g) question, housing, climate, taxes) were not found in her campaign materials or press coverage as of this research; only positions with direct sourcing are included above.
